sections.text: What Are Medicare Part B Excess Charges?

sections.content: A Medicare Part B excess charge happens when a doctor or provider who does not accept [Medicare assignment](/faqs/what-is-medicare-assignment/) bills you more than the [Medicare-approved amount](/faqs/medicare-part-b-premiums/) for a covered service. Under federal rules, these [non-participating providers](/faqs/medicare-coverage-for-mental-health/) can charge up to 15% above the Medicare-approved amount, a cap known as the [limiting charge](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/medicare-costs/provider-accept-Medicare). That extra 15% is the excess charge, and unless you have coverage that protects against it, you are responsible for paying it yourself.

This rule applies only to Part B services, meaning outpatient care, doctor visits, and other medical services billed under Part B. It does not apply to Part A hospital costs, which follow different billing and assignment rules.

Excess charges do not apply to every appointment you book. Most providers who treat Medicare patients accept assignment, so this situation comes up in specific circumstances rather than as a routine part of using Original Medicare.

sections.calloutText:
Excess charges only happen when a non-participating provider doesn't accept Medicare assignment, and they're capped at 15% above the Medicare-approved amount.
[Plan F and Plan G](/faqs/what-is-a-medicare-supplement-plan-and-who-needs-one/) are the only standardized [Medigap plans](/faqs/medicare-supplement-plans/medigap-plans/) that currently cover this cost, though Plan F is closed to those newly eligible for Medicare on or after January 1, 2020.
Before a planned procedure or specialist visit, ask the billing office whether the provider accepts assignment so you can avoid an unexpected bill.

sections.text: Why Some Doctors Charge Excess Fees

sections.content: Providers who work with Medicare generally fall into three categories, and understanding the difference helps explain where [excess charges](/faqs/part-b-excess-charges-medicare-overcharge-measure/) come from.

items: Participating providers agree to accept the Medicare-approved amount as full payment for every service, so there is no excess charge risk with them.

Non-participating providers can still treat Medicare patients but are not required to accept assignment on every claim, which means they can bill up to the 15% limiting charge above the approved amount.

Providers who opt out of Medicare entirely do not bill Medicare at all; instead, you pay them directly under a private contract, and Medicare rules on limiting charges do not apply in that arrangement.

sections.content: Accepting assignment means a provider agrees to be paid directly by Medicare and accepts the Medicare-approved amount as payment in full, aside from your normal coinsurance or deductible. Some providers choose not to accept assignment because it allows them to bill patients more for certain services, particularly in specialties where demand is high or reimbursement rates feel low relative to their costs.

This practice is not widespread across all of Medicare, but it shows up more often with certain specialists, such as some psychiatrists or other providers in fields where non-participation is more common. It is worth asking about assignment status when you are selecting a new specialist, rather than assuming every provider in your network bills the same way.

sections.text: How Much Can Excess Charges Really Cost You?

sections.content: The limiting charge is calculated as 15% above the Medicare-approved amount for the specific service you received, not 15% above whatever the provider decides to bill. For example, if the Medicare-approved amount for a service is $100, a non-participating provider who does not accept assignment could legally charge up to $115, the extra $15 being the excess charge.

Without a Medigap plan that covers this cost, that extra amount comes entirely out of your pocket, on top of your normal Part B coinsurance. Because the exact dollar impact depends on the service, the provider, and the Medicare-approved amount for that specific billing code, there is no single number that applies to every situation.

Before a planned procedure or a visit with a new specialist, it is reasonable to ask the provider's billing office two things: whether they accept Medicare assignment, and what the Medicare-approved amount is for the service you need. This small step turns a potentially unpredictable bill into something you can plan for ahead of time, which matters under Original Medicare since there is no yearly out-of-pocket maximum built into Parts A and B on their own.

sections.text: Which Medigap Plans Cover Part B Excess Charges?

sections.content: Among the standardized Medigap plans, only two currently include coverage for Part B excess charges.

items: Plan F covers excess charges in full, but it is closed to anyone newly eligible for Medicare on or after January 1, 2020.
Plan G also covers excess charges in full and remains available to new enrollees, making it the primary option for people who want this protection going forward.

sections.content: Other standardized Medigap plans may not include this benefit, so it is worth confirming the details directly with [MedicareFAQ](/medicare-supplement-plans/plan-g/) or by reviewing your plan's benefit summary before you enroll. This distinction matters most for beneficiaries who regularly see specialists, since those are the visits where a non-participating provider is more likely to come up.

sections.text: How Plan N Treats Excess Charges Differently

sections.content: Plan N is often attractive for its lower premium compared to Plan G, and it [pays 100% of Part B coinsurance costs](https://www.medicare.gov/health-drug-plans/medigap/basics/compare-plan-benefits), though it does require small copayments, up to $20 for some office visits and up to $50 for emergency room visits when you are not admitted as an inpatient.

However, Plan N does not include the same excess charge protection built into Plan F or Plan G. If you see a non-participating provider while enrolled in Plan N, the excess charge portion of the bill could still land on you. If you are weighing Plan N against Plan G mainly for the premium savings, it is worth considering how often you see specialists and whether those providers accept assignment before deciding.

If you are torn between Plan G and Plan N, ask yourself how often you see specialists outside your regular primary care network. If you rarely see non-participating providers, Plan N's lower premium may make sense. If you see several specialists a year, the excess charge protection in Plan G can offer more predictable costs even with a higher monthly premium.

sections.text: Can You Still Get Excess Charge Coverage If Plans F and C Are Closed?

sections.content: Plans C and F are not available to people who became newly eligible for Medicare on or after January 1, 2020, a change that applies regardless of when you actually enroll. If you turned 65 or otherwise qualified for Medicare after that date, these two plans are not on the table for you.

There is a notable exception: if you [were eligible for Medicare before January 1, 2020, but hadn't yet signed up](https://www.medicare.gov/publications/02110-choosing-a-medigap-policy.pdf?ftag=MSFd61514f#page=19), you may still be able to buy Plan C or Plan F if it is offered in your state. This applies to a narrower group of people whose eligibility window started earlier but who delayed enrollment.

For most newly eligible beneficiaries, Plan G remains the practical path to excess charge coverage, since it offers the same protection as Plan F without the eligibility restriction. Before assuming you are locked out of any option, confirm your specific eligibility date and plan availability in your state with a licensed agent, since these details can be easy to misjudge on your own.

sections.text: Weighing the Premium Cost of Excess Charge Coverage

sections.content: Medigap plans with broader coverage, including Plan F and Plan G, generally carry higher monthly premiums than plans that leave out benefits like excess charge protection. This is the general tradeoff built into how these plans are priced: more comprehensive coverage tends to cost more upfront in exchange for fewer surprises later.

Whether that tradeoff makes sense for you depends on your own healthcare habits. If you rarely see specialists, or if the providers you use consistently accept assignment, the added premium for excess charge coverage may matter less to your overall budget. If you see multiple specialists a year or anticipate needing care from providers whose assignment status you are unsure of, that protection can offset a higher premium over time.

Because exact premium pricing varies by your location, age, and the insurance carrier offering the plan, it is worth getting a personalized quote rather than relying on general assumptions about what Plan F, Plan G, or Plan N might cost in your area.

sections.text: How to Check If Your Provider Accepts Medicare Assignment

sections.content: Confirming a provider's assignment status before an appointment is one of the simplest ways to avoid an unexpected excess charge.

items: Ask the provider's billing staff directly whether they accept Medicare assignment for the service you need.
Use Medicare's online physician comparison tool to check a provider's participation status before scheduling.
Get written confirmation of assignment status before a non-routine procedure, especially if it involves a new specialist or a planned surgery.

sections.content: This step matters most when you are seeing a new specialist for the first time or scheduling a procedure that is not part of your routine care, since those are the situations where assignment status is less likely to be something you already know. A few minutes of checking ahead of time can prevent a bill that catches you off guard weeks later.

sections.text: Getting Help Choosing the Right Medigap Plan

sections.content: Licensed agents at MedicareFAQ can compare Medigap plans side by side based on your doctors, your budget, and your expected healthcare needs, including whether excess charge coverage makes sense for your situation. The goal is to give you clear answers to your specific questions, not to push you toward a particular plan.

Comparing your options with someone who understands how these plans differ can help you avoid a costly mismatch, like choosing a lower-premium plan only to find out later that it does not cover a cost you end up facing regularly.

sections.text: Frequently Asked Questions About Medicare Part B Excess Charges

faqs.question: What are Medicare Part B excess charges, in simple terms?
faqs.answer: They are extra amounts a non-participating Medicare provider can legally bill above the Medicare-approved amount, up to 15% more, when that provider does not accept assignment. This only applies to Part B services and only when you see a provider who does not accept assignment, not to every visit.

faqs.question: Are there limits on Medicare Part B excess charges?
faqs.answer: Yes, the limiting charge caps excess fees at 15% above the Medicare-approved amount, and this cap applies only to non-participating providers. Providers who fully opt out of Medicare are not bound by this limit, since they bill under a private contract instead.

faqs.question: I'm not ready to talk to anyone yet, can I just read more first?
faqs.answer: Yes, taking time to research on your own is a reasonable approach. You can continue exploring Medigap topics and plan comparisons on MedicareFAQ whenever it fits your timeline, with no obligation to speak with an agent until you have questions you want answered directly.

faqs.question: Will I get a pushy sales call if I ask about Medigap plans?
faqs.answer: MedicareFAQ's approach focuses on education first, answering your specific questions rather than pressuring you toward a decision. Licensed agents are available when you want to compare plans, but reaching out does not commit you to anything.

faqs.question: How do I know which source to trust for Medicare information?
faqs.answer: Official sources like Medicare.gov provide the baseline rules for coverage, costs, and eligibility. Pairing that with guidance from a licensed Medicare agent who can apply those rules to your specific doctors, prescriptions, and budget gives you a more complete picture than either source alone.

faqs.question: What happens if I choose the wrong Medigap plan?
faqs.answer: Switching Medigap plans later is possible, but outside certain guaranteed-issue periods, you may need to go through medical underwriting, which could affect your ability to switch or your premium. Getting guidance before you enroll can reduce the chances of needing to make a change later.

faqs.question: Does every doctor who doesn't accept assignment charge the full 15%?
faqs.answer: No, the 15% limiting charge is a maximum, not a guaranteed amount every non-participating provider charges. Actual excess charges vary by provider and by service, so it is worth confirming the specific amount with the billing office rather than assuming the full 15% applies.

faqs.question: Can I switch to a plan that covers excess charges later if I change my mind?
faqs.answer: Switching is generally possible, but outside a guaranteed-issue period, the new carrier may require medical underwriting before approving your application. A licensed agent can walk you through your specific options and timing if you are considering a change.

sections.text: Your Next Step Toward Confident Medigap Coverage

sections.content: Understanding how Part B excess charges work gives you a clearer picture of where surprise bills can come from and which Medigap plans close that gap. With that knowledge, you can compare Plan G or Plan F against other options while keeping your own doctors, specialists, and budget in view.

When you are ready, MedicareFAQ can walk through a no-pressure comparison of your Medigap options based on your specific situation, so you can choose coverage with a clear understanding of what it does and does not include.

claims.claim: Medicare Part B excess charges arise when a non-participating provider doesn't accept assignment and charges up to 15% above the Medicare-approved amount, known as the 'limiting charge'.
claims.reason: Source confirms the limiting charge definition matching the claim.

evidence.quote: In many cases, the charge can't be more than 15% above the Medicare-approved amount for non-participating healthcare providers. This amount is called "the limiting charge."

claims.claim: Among standardized Medigap plans, only Plan F and Plan G cover Part B excess charges; Plans A, B, C, D, K, L, M, and N do not cover this charge.
claims.reason: No source lists which standardized plans cover or exclude Part B excess charges beyond Plan N; no comprehensive comparison of A,B,C,D,K,L,M is provided.

claims.claim: Plan N does not cover Part B excess charges, but it does pay 100% of Part B coinsurance costs (subject to small copayments for some office and ER visits).

evidence.quote: Plan N pays 100% of the costs of Part B coinsurance. You must pay a copayment of up to $20 for some office visits and up to $50 for emergency room visits when you aren't admitted as an inpatient.

articleBrief.audience: Medicare beneficiaries and soon-to-be-eligible consumers researching Medigap coverage, particularly those considering providers who may not accept Medicare assignment, and caregivers helping them choose a plan
articleBrief.purpose: Explain what Medicare Part B excess charges are, how they can affect out-of-pocket costs, and which Medigap (Medicare Supplement) plans provide coverage for them, so readers can make an informed decision when selecting a Medigap plan
articleBrief.questions:
What exactly is a Medicare Part B excess charge, and how is it calculated?
Why do some doctors charge excess fees, and how common is this practice?
Which Medigap plans cover Part B excess charges, and which do not?
How much can excess charges actually cost a beneficiary without this coverage?
Is it still possible to enroll in a Medigap plan that covers excess charges if Plans F and C are closed to new Medicare beneficiaries?
How does covering excess charges affect the overall premium cost of a Medigap plan?
articleBrief.scope: Cover: definition of Part B excess charges and the 15% legal limit under Medicare assignment rules; explanation of 'non-participating' providers and assignment; which Medigap plans currently cover excess charges (Plan F and Plan G, noting Plan C and F are closed to those newly eligible after Jan 1, 2020); how Plan N differs in its excess charge treatment; cost/premium tradeoffs of choosing a plan with this coverage; practical guidance on checking if a provider accepts assignment; brief mention of how MedicareFAQ can help compare Medigap plans. Leave out: detailed state-by-state Medigap pricing, unrelated Medigap benefits (e.g., foreign travel emergency, Part A deductible) beyond brief context, Medicare Advantage plan comparisons, and enrollment period mechanics unless directly tied to plan availability for excess charge coverage.
articleBrief.formatReason: The topic asks readers to understand a concept (what Part B excess charges are) and then know which Medigap plans cover them. This requires a direct definitional answer plus supporting explanation, examples, and exceptions rather than a ranking, comparison table, or task-based steps.

excerpt: Medicare Part B excess charges occur when non-participating providers bill up to 15% above the Medicare-approved amount. Learn how they work and how to avoid them.
keyTakeaways: Excess charges apply only to Part B services from non-participating providers who don't accept Medicare assignment
Federal law caps these charges at 15% above the Medicare-approved amount, known as the limiting charge
Plan F and Plan G are the only Medigap plans that currently cover excess charges
Plan F is no longer available to those newly eligible for Medicare on or after January 1, 2020
Ask your provider's billing office about assignment status before appointments to avoid unexpected costs
